The last time WTI prices broke the $100 per barrel mark was in May, after which they fell following the announcement of an interim peace agreement with Iran. That agreement has since expired, and global markets are responding as hostilities continue.
The West Texas Intermediate price of oil, the U.S. benchmark, hit $101.53 per barrel Thursday morning.
The last time WTI prices broke the $100 per barrel mark was in May. They fell to pre-war levels in early July following the announcement of an interim peace agreement with Iran. That agreement has since expired, and global markets are responding as hostilities continue.
President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday before he headed into the Republican Party's midterm convention that the war in Iran would end "immediately after the election," CNBC reported. Trump also said energy prices would, right after the election, begin "tumbling down."
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing unnamed sources, that top White House advisors have discussed with Trump the possibility the war would drag on through the remainder of his term. President Donald Trump heckled the leaders of Iran at the first-ever Republican midterm convention on Wednesday, while promoting the idea of renaming the Strait of Hormuz after himself.
“The war will be over very shortly after the election,” Trump said in a 100-minute address. “They’re hanging out for dear life, hoping that we lose, so they can deal with dumb, weak Democrats, and they can have their nuclear bomb. But we’re not going to let that happen.”
The president expressed confidence that Iran is “going to be quitting or dropping out” of the war “right after Election Day, because they want a deal desperately.”
“We’re winning it,” Trump said, referring to the war in Iran. “We control the Hormuz Strait.”
The U.S. and Israel started the war in February 2026. Since then, Trump has repeatedly predicted victory or an imminent end to the conflict. But six months later, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted amid competing U.S. and Iranian efforts to control the vital waterway.
On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 10 ships near the strait after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the largest exchange of attacks on shipping by the two sides since the war began.
“I should get something out of this — the Trump Strait,” the president continued, repeating an idea he had proposed about a week ago. “I’ll have an announcement. We’ll call it the Trump Strait, and I’m sure the Iranian leadership will be thrilled with that.”
Declaring that they’re probably not “too happy about anything,” Trump said that Iran “is falling apart” and described the country as “the bully of the Middle East.”
“They’re not the bully anymore,” the president continued. “We’re the hottest country anywhere in the world.”

Iran war won't end until after crucial November elections, says Trump
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.
"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday.
He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the Republican Party's first midterm election convention – and repeated them there, arguing that short-term economic pain was worth it to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
The conflict rapidly spread across the Middle East, as Iran retaliated by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Arab states hosting US military facilities.
The price of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, has risen above the $100 (£74) mark three times over the past six months, with Iranian attacks forcing production stoppages in Gulf states and disrupting exports through the vital Strait of Hormuz waterway.
The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran's ports and has recently begun striking Iranian tankers in response to attacks on warships and other vessels.
"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."
He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" – an apparent reference to the Democrats – "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".
He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons and insisted its nuclear programme is solely peaceful.
At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".
In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".
Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".
The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from fuel to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings – and pressure from those within his party, including staunch supporters, to quickly end the war.
Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing control on Congress.
At the convention, Trump sought to energise the party ahead of November. Historically, a sitting president's party tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterm elections.
Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and other goods that require shipping.
The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July. Similarly, earlier this week the price of US diesel hit an all-time high, which is likely to cause a ripple effect on prices across the US.
There are also predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates.
On Tuesday night, the US military said it had attacked and destroyed five oil tankers with ties to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) in the Gulf of Oman and the northern Gulf.
The IRGC, in response, said early on Wednesday that its naval forces had attacked two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels. Centcom denied its warships were hit.
The IRGC also said it had launched ballistic missiles at US military maintenance facilities, hangars and aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.
Jordan's armed forces said they intercepted 20 Iranian missiles and that two other missiles fell in unpopulated areas with no casualties reported.
Later on Wednesday, sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that several US fighter jets at the air base were damaged in the Iranian strikes.
One A-10 Thunderbolt aircraft was hit and was missing a wing, and about eight F-15s sustained light damage, according to people familiar with the matter.
Explosions were reported in southern Iran on Wednesday night, but Iranian official sources denied they were US strikes, saying the sounds came from the sea.
In a separate development on Tuesday, the Iran-backed Houthi movement in Yemen launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, causing fires at several oil facilities.
Saudi media reported more Houthi attacks on the kingdom on Wednesday, citing a military spokesman as condemning missile and drone strikes on the cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan.
The Houthis have said they are retaliating for days of Saudi air strikes on their territory in western Yemen, where a four-year-old informal ceasefire has collapsed.

Trump Predicts Iran War Will End After Midterms as Oil and Fuel Prices Climb
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he expects the war with Iran to end shortly after the Nov. 3 midterm elections and predicted oil prices will then begin falling, as gasoline, diesel and crude prices remain elevated.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
President Donald Trump predicted Wednesday that the war with Iran will end shortly after the 2026 midterm elections, arguing that Tehran is trying to endure the conflict until the Nov. 3 vote while Americans continue facing sharply higher fuel prices.
Speaking with reporters before traveling to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump said he expects oil prices to begin declining after Election Day.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”
Trump accused Iran of attempting to influence the U.S. political environment by prolonging the conflict.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
“I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer,” he added.
The president offered no specific diplomatic or military development supporting the timetable, making the statement a prediction rather than an announced agreement or ceasefire plan. The U.S.-Iran conflict is now in its seventh month, and renewed attacks around the Strait of Hormuz pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel Wednesday.
The conflict has sharply disrupted petroleum shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global petroleum moved before the war. Brent crude settled at $101.21 Wednesday after renewed attacks involving U.S. and Iranian vessels intensified concerns about global supplies.
American motorists are increasingly feeling the impact.
Regular gasoline averaged $4.15 per gallon nationally over Labor Day, compared with approximately $3.20 a year earlier. By Wednesday, the national average had climbed further to about $4.22 per gallon. Diesel reached approximately $5.94 per gallon, up sharply from year-ago levels.
U.S. consumers have paid an estimated $100 billion in additional gasoline and diesel expenses since the war began, equivalent to roughly $760 per household, according to a real-time estimate from Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs. The estimate continues rising as elevated energy prices persist.
The administration has taken several steps intended to increase fuel supplies and limit price increases. The Environmental Protection Agency last month accelerated the transition to winter-grade gasoline, allowing less restrictive federal volatility standards beginning Sept. 1 rather than waiting until the normal end of the summer fuel season.
The United States has also drawn from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. By early August, the reserve had fallen below 300 million barrels, more than 100 million barrels lower than at the beginning of 2026, according to reporting on the administration’s response to the war-driven supply disruptions.
Trump’s comments place the conflict’s potential end beyond the midterm elections even as fighting and oil-market disruptions continue. Vice President JD Vance last week declined to offer a similar timetable, saying he did not want to impose “artificial timelines” on the war and could not predict when Iran would stop its attacks.
For now, Trump is forecasting that both the military conflict and the pressure it has placed on energy markets will ease after November, while oil traders and consumers continue confronting prices driven by an unresolved war and instability around one of the world’s most important petroleum shipping routes.

He stated, “Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers.”
The economic fallout from this conflict is becoming impossible to ignore. The disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has caused oil prices to surge, with the international Brent crude oil benchmark climbing past $100 a barrel for the first time since July. While this shift is clearly impacting the economy, President Trump has previously downplayed the price spike, arguing that costs will drop significantly once the war is over.

President Donald Trump believes the war with Iran could end almost immediately after America’s November midterm elections. His reasoning is straightforward: Tehran is running out of options.
Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Trump argued that Iran is deliberately trying to prolong the conflict in hopes of influencing American politics. According to the president, Tehran wants American voters to empower politicians who will ease the military and economic pressure and allow the Islamic Republic to preserve its nuclear ambitions.
“I think the war will end immediately after the election,” Trump said, arguing that Iran simply “can’t hold out any longer.”
That assessment highlights something much larger than American electoral politics.
For decades, Iran built its strategy around patience. Tehran constructed a regional network of proxies, invested heavily in ballistic missiles, pursued nuclear capabilities, and assumed that Western governments would eventually tire of confrontation.
That calculation may finally be collapsing.
The United States is no longer limiting itself to sanctions and diplomatic warnings. Trump said American strikes overnight destroyed nine Iranian ships—and warned that there is more coming.
More importantly, Trump made clear that Washington’s objectives have expanded.
This is no longer simply about negotiating another nuclear agreement. Trump said any future arrangement would demand “much more than a nuclear deal,” with additional issues placed on the negotiating table that were not being discussed only months ago.
That is precisely where the strategic opportunity lies.
Iran’s nuclear program is extraordinarily important, but the threat never stopped there. Tehran’s missile arsenal, terrorist proxies, attacks on international shipping, and decades-long campaign against Israel are all parts of the same revolutionary strategy.
The mistake would be allowing Iran to survive this confrontation, regroup, and rebuild.
If Tehran wants an end to the war, the objective should not simply be another temporary agreement.
It should be an Iran that can no longer threaten Israel, America, or the region.

The resolution was backed by 23 of the board’s 35 member states, with Russia, China and Niger voting against, eight abstaining and one not participating.
The referral is not expected to produce immediate sanctions because Russia and China, both Iranian allies and permanent members of the Security Council, could block such measures. Still, sending the issue to the UN’s most powerful body marks a significant diplomatic escalation and follows an IAEA resolution adopted on June 12, 2025, one day before Israel launched its war against Iran, which found Tehran in violation of its nonproliferation commitments.
The dispute centers in part on long-running IAEA investigations into uranium traces found at undeclared Iranian sites and Tehran’s refusal to allow inspectors full access to facilities damaged in the war. Much of the material was reportedly buried underground near the damaged Isfahan facility, while Iran has denied inspectors access to Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow.

He added, "Originally I wanted to make a deal [with Iran]. We're so far down the line. They have very little country left right now. So we're not looking for, yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it's not something we're looking at. This war will end immediately after our election."
New Air Force One Slide Deployed
Trump arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Marine One, with reporters on the ground stating that he had to wait on board the helicopter for a short time. An emergency slide was spotted deployed from the new Qatari-gifted Air Force One, with photos showing staff moving around underneath the plane.
A short time later, the old Air Force One was maneuvered out of its hangar into position a short distance away.
The White House declined to comment further when reached by Newsweek.
Trump's Claims About the End of the War
Trump's remarks marked one of his clearest predictions yet about the duration of the conflict. At the outset of the war, the president said the fighting would last only weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month.
Trump has offered an imminent or relatively near-term end to the conflict at least two dozen times, after initially estimating four to five weeks. Wednesday's forecast is materially different because it effectively extends the timeline until after November 3, almost eight months after the fighting began.
Over the course of the war, since it began at the end of February, there have been at least 23 separate dates on which Trump said the conflict was short, nearly finished, would end soon or within a specified period, or had effectively been won.
Speaking to Newsweek later in the afternoon, Florida GOP Chair Evan Power reflected on the president's remarks, saying, "The Iranian regime has been on 47 years, they've been in power, they've killed countless American lives through their terrorism network.
"The president took both decisive action by in an election year to go after and change that regime," Power said. "And I think when you look at it, it pays long term benefits, because that's going to provide real peace in that region, and that will end up in lower gas prices long term."
Gas Prices Since the War Began
When the conflict began on February 28, the national average for regular gasoline was approximately $2.982 per gallon, according to Brown University’s Iran War Energy Cost Tracker, which uses AAA daily averages. As of Wednesday afternoon, the tracker showed $4.147, up $1.165 per gallon, or 39.1 percent.
The latest Associated Press report, citing AAA, puts the current national average slightly higher, at $4.22 per gallon, up 7 cents overnight. Against the $2.982 war-start figure, that represents an increase of approximately $1.24 per gallon, or 41.5 percent. The AP also reports that gasoline is now more than $1 a gallon higher than at the same point last year.
Diesel has risen even more sharply. Brown’s tracker shows the national average rising from $3.670 on February 28 to $5.882, a 60.3 percent increase. The AP’s latest figure is $5.94, described as a record high. That matters beyond motorists because diesel prices feed into trucking, delivery and production expenses.
Oil itself has been volatile. On Wednesday, international Brent crude moved back above $100 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate reached around $95 to $96, following renewed U.S.-Iran attacks. Trump said oil prices would come “tumbling downward” after the election, linking the expected decline to an end to the war.
Florida Senator Rick Scott, speaking to CBS News Wednesday, challenged the concerns over gas prices, saying, "Nobody likes war, nobody likes higher gas prices, but nobody wants to be killed by a nuclear weapon. That's what's at stake here. Do we want to be destroyed by a nuclear weapon?"
Inflation Since February
The inflation rate was 2.4 percent in February, just before the war’s economic effects began showing up in economic data. It accelerated to 3.3 percent in March, reached 4.2 percent in May, and then eased to 3.5 percent in June and 3.4 percent in July.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose from 326.785 in February to 333.918 in July, meaning average consumer prices were about 2.2 percent higher by July.
The latest official inflation report is for July, because the August CPI will not be released until September 11.

Trump also spoke at length about the war in Iran during his keynote address to the convention Wednesday evening. He acknowledged it caused energy prices to spike and financial markets to struggle, but said it was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Washington (GNP): US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the war with Iran would end immediately after the US midterm elections in November, as renewed fighting pushed oil prices above $100 a barrel and raised concerns over disruption to global energy supplies.
Speaking to reporters before travelling to Dallas for a Republican Party midterm convention, Trump said he believed the war would end right after the election because Iran could not hold out any longer. He did not explain the basis for this expectation but said Tehran was seeking to influence the outcome of the vote, arguing that Iran wanted a weaker US government that would leave it alone and allow it to pursue a nuclear weapon. The conflict, which began in February and is now in its seventh month, has shown no clear sign of ending, with both sides continuing to exchange attacks even as diplomatic efforts have yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Trump also predicted that US energy prices, which have risen sharply during the conflict, would fall after the midterms, saying he expected gasoline prices to drop below two dollars a gallon. He said the higher prices were a consequence of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, and when asked about elevated gasoline costs, said Americans needed only to consider whether they were prepared to allow Iran to acquire one.
He further claimed Iran was in shambles and suffering from severe inflation, reiterating his assertion that the United States controls the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for global oil and gas shipments.
The president’s remarks came as oil prices surged on Wednesday amid the intensifying conflict. Brent crude futures rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since July 24, reaching as high as $101.58 before easing, while US West Texas Intermediate crude climbed to its highest level since early June.
The rise followed attacks on oil tankers and growing concern over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply passed before the war began. Shipping volumes through the strait have fallen well below pre-war levels, with preliminary data showing only six commodity vessels passing through the waterway on Tuesday compared with a 10-day average of about 12.
The US Energy Information Administration has raised its price forecasts as the conflict drains global inventories, projecting Brent crude to average about $91 a barrel in 2026 and WTI to average about $84.65 a barrel, forecasts finalised on September 3 before the latest escalation. The disruption has also pushed European natural gas prices higher, with the Dutch TTF benchmark rising above 80 euros per megawatt-hour on Wednesday, its highest level since early 2023.

Rystad Energy chief economist Claudio Galimberti said flows through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen from around 8 to 9 million barrels per day before fighting resumed on August 30 to below 2 million barrels per day more recently, while Abaxx Markets co-chairman Jeffrey Currie said the rise in energy prices reflected a structural shift rather than a temporary shock.
Military activity has escalated alongside the economic fallout. The US military said on Wednesday it had destroyed 10 Iranian oil tankers over the past week, describing them as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network financing Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. US Central Command said the vessels, identified as the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya, were struck after the Revolutionary Guard targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over two days, adding that crews were ordered to abandon the tankers before they were rendered inoperable and that the warship evaded both attacks without American casualties.
Central Command separately rejected an Iranian claim that its forces had struck two US Navy destroyers, saying no US warship had been hit and that all attempted Iranian attacks had failed. The latest destruction followed the sinking of five other Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday and three more on September 7, after what the command described as further Revolutionary Guard attempts to target a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
Iran has warned against continued US attacks, with Brigadier General Ramezan Sharif, a senior Revolutionary Guard adviser, telling state broadcaster Press TV that Iran was monitoring the region and that further US strikes could trigger unique Iranian responses, describing the Strait of Hormuz as a strategic and deterrent weapon for Tehran.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said on Wednesday its naval forces had attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf in retaliation for the destruction of the five Iranian tankers, claiming heavy damage without identifying the vessels involved, and said it had also targeted 10 other vessels attempting to enter what it called a prohibited and unsafe area of the strait. Separately, Iranian state news agency Fars reported that an explosion was heard off the southern port city of Jask, without providing details on its cause.
The confrontation has extended beyond military targets to commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz, marking the largest declared wave of tit-for-tat strikes on shipping since the war began. The oil products tanker Hercules Star was attacked while at anchor off Dubai, killing one crew member and leaving another missing, with maritime security sources suggesting the vessel may have been struck by a drone.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said it had received reports of several merchant vessels struck by disabling fire in the Gulf of Oman, while Iraqi port officials said the tanker New Andros, carrying about two million barrels of fuel oil, caught fire after being struck by a drone in Iraqi waters, though no casualties were reported among its 22 crew members.
Traffic through the strait has fallen sharply since the escalation, with Iran largely choking off transit and Washington imposing a blockade of Iranian ports, though the United States says it has continued guiding tankers through the waterway.

sources.text:
Trump warns oil prices may remain high until after US midterms
The president linked elevated crude prices to the ongoing Iran conflict and predicted they would 'tumble downward' after November's elections.
President Trump told reporters on September 9 that Americans should expect oil and gas prices to stay elevated through the November midterm elections, attributing the sustained pressure to the US-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets for most of 2026.
Speaking before departing for Texas and the Republican Party’s midterm convention, Trump predicted that prices would “tumble downward” once the elections are behind us.
The numbers behind the pain
Brent crude climbed above $100 per barrel on the same day Trump made his remarks. The national average gasoline price sat at $4.22 per gallon, a figure that has become frustratingly familiar to American drivers.
Gas prices have exceeded $4 per gallon frequently throughout 2026. At the worst point of the conflict, WTI crude surged above $112 per barrel.
The US-Iran conflict, which began on February 28, 2026, has repeatedly disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. That narrow waterway handles roughly 20% of the world’s oil supply. Houthi attacks on shipping routes have compounded the problem, adding another layer of risk premium to every barrel moving through the region.
A political problem dressed up as an energy crisis
The administration has not been idle. Trump has engaged directly with major refiners and fuel retailers to try to ease the burden on consumers.
For voters, the math is simple. A family driving 1,000 miles per month in a vehicle averaging 25 miles per gallon is spending roughly $169 per month on gas at current prices.
What markets are watching
A reopening of normal Strait of Hormuz traffic could pull Brent crude back toward the $70-$80 range relatively quickly, given that non-conflict fundamentals don’t support triple-digit oil.
The sustained period of elevated energy costs has broader economic implications beyond the pump. Higher fuel prices feed into transportation and logistics costs, which ripple into consumer goods pricing. Major oil producers tend to post outsized earnings when crude stays above $90.
